title: So much solar: Digging into the list of every US power plant that went online this year
gist: EIA data on the 368 US utility-scale power plants that came online January-June 2026 shows solar (11,458 MW across 207 projects) and batteries (8,207 MW across 95 projects) dominating actual completions, while headline wind and combined-cycle gas projects are legacy artifacts; Texas, New Mexico and Arizona took roughly half of new capacity and the announced gas boom is still years out.

themes.theme: What actually got built in H1 2026

insights.claim: 368 US utility-scale power plants began operation between January and June 2026 according to EIA data, and the group is dominated by utility-scale solar.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Completions data, unlike interconnection queues or announcements, is the only hard read on where power-sector capex is actually landing.
insights.quote: the list of 368 utility-scale plants that began operation from January to June
insights.locator: At times of rapid change, forecasting is difficult

insights.claim: By project count in H1 2026, utility-scale solar led with 207 projects, batteries followed with 95, natural gas combustion turbines had 22, natural gas internal combustion engines 21, and onshore wind just nine.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Project-count breadth favors developers and EPCs serving many small solar+storage sites over turbine-scale contractors.
insights.locator: Utility-scale solar led in the number of projects coming online

insights.claim: By generating capacity added in H1 2026, utility-scale solar led with 11,458 MW, batteries added 8,207 MW, onshore wind 5,473 MW (mostly SunZia), and the three largest natural gas plant types added only 2,707 MW combined.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Gas added roughly a quarter of what solar did despite the gas-buildout narrative — a check on near-term gas turbine and gas-demand enthusiasm.
insights.locator: If we look at projects in terms of generating capacity

insights.claim: Small-scale and rooftop solar is excluded from the EIA utility-scale database, meaning the reported solar totals understate total US solar additions.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Anyone sizing total solar demand from this dataset is systematically low; residential installers sit outside these numbers.
insights.quote: Small-scale solar, including rooftop solar, is not part of this database.
insights.locator: Small-scale solar, including rooftop solar

themes.theme: Headline projects are echoes, not trends

insights.claim: SunZia Wind South and SunZia Wind North in New Mexico came online in spring 2026 as the largest US wind farms with 3,650 MW combined, but the project took about a decade to build and signals a past boom rather than a current onshore wind revival.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate onshore wind demand from record capacity headlines; the development pipeline behind them has already dried up.
insights.quote: the SunZia is not indicative of an onshore wind-energy boom. It is more like an echo from a past boom.
insights.locator: This is a top-heavy list, led by SunZia Wind South

insights.claim: US onshore wind development has dwindled for reasons tied to regulation and public opinion, a trend visible in Texas — the national leader in onshore wind — bringing zero new wind projects online in the first half of 2026.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Wind turbine OEMs and onshore wind yieldcos face a structurally shrinking US addressable market even in the friendliest state.
insights.quote: The state is the national leader in onshore wind, but brought no new projects online in the first half of the year.
insights.locator: Also, Texas illustrates how challenging the market is for new onshore wind

insights.claim: Vineyard Wind, the offshore wind project near Massachusetts, was the fourth-largest new plant of H1 2026 but, like SunZia, spent so long in development that its completion says little about future offshore trends.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Offshore wind completions are lagging indicators; forward offshore capex should be judged from new starts, not ribbon-cuttings.
insights.locator: The fourth-largest new power plant

insights.claim: Green River Energy Center in Utah — 800 MW comprising 400 MW of solar and 400 MW of batteries — was the fifth-largest new plant and the first on the list that reflects the actual prevailing build trend.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: The 1:1 solar-to-battery pairing at utility scale is becoming the template configuration to underwrite.
insights.locator: It isn't until the fifth-largest new plant

insights.claim: Energy Innovation senior fellow Eric Gimon argues the bulk of new US generation is small and mid-size utility-scale solar that draws no attention but is being built almost everywhere, frequently paired with batteries.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Value accrues to standardized, repeatable mid-size projects and their supply chain rather than to megaproject developers.
insights.quote: The real underlying workhorse is solar plus battery
insights.locator: One of Gimon's takeaways is that we're firmly in the era of utility-scale solar

insights.claim: Smaller-size solar projects win because they are easier to build and because siting options for them are far more numerous and diverse than for large plants.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Permitting and land-access friction, not module cost, is the binding constraint that favors modular solar over megaprojects.
insights.quote: These kinds of smaller-size projects are just easier to build, and the site possibilities are much more diverse and easy to find
insights.locator: Gimon explained that the bulk of new projects are small and mid-size

insights.claim: Comparing generating capacity across technologies is misleading because solar produces nothing at night and many gas plants only run a few days or weeks per year to cover peak demand.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Nameplate-MW comparisons overstate solar's energy contribution and understate peaker economics — model capacity factor, not headline MW.
insights.locator: A perpetual caveat: Power plant technologies have important differences

themes.theme: Geography and state policy as the real driver

insights.claim: Texas, New Mexico and Arizona together accounted for about half of all new US generating capacity brought online in the first half of 2026.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Power-sector construction exposure is highly concentrated in the Southwest — regional interconnect and land plays follow that concentration.
insights.locator: Three states account for about half of the country's new generating capacity

insights.claim: In Texas the leading new-capacity category in H1 2026 was batteries at 3,067 MW, ahead of utility-scale solar at 2,311 MW and gas combustion turbines or internal combustion engines at 1,154 MW, reflecting state policies prioritizing gas and battery construction for grid reliability at high demand.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: ERCOT is now a battery-first market; storage revenue stacks and ancillary pricing there are the leading indicator for US storage economics.
insights.quote: Texas' policies have prioritized gas and battery plant construction to help bolster the power grid's reliability at times of high demand.
insights.locator: Texas was the leader, with a power mix

insights.claim: Illinois ranked first nationally in the number of new utility-scale solar projects with 36, ahead of California's 22 and Texas' 16, yet barely cracked the top 10 in capacity because its projects are small — evidence that state laws encouraging small and medium-size solar actually produce completed projects.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: State policy design, not resource quality, determines completion rates — a screen for where distributed-scale solar developers can reliably close projects.
insights.quote: This is policy-driven and shows that state laws encouraging small and medium-size solar are leading to completed projects.
insights.locator: Illinois ranked first in the number of new utility-scale solar projects

themes.theme: The gas buildout is deferred, not cancelled

insights.claim: Only three combined-cycle natural gas plants came online in H1 2026 despite massive announced combined-cycle capacity in development, because the high tide of new gas plants is still a few years away.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Gas turbine backlog converts to revenue late-decade, not now — a timing risk for anyone marking gas-buildout theses to current completions.
insights.quote: The high tide of new gas plants won't arrive for another few years.
insights.locator: Combined-cycle natural gas, despite having massive amounts

insights.claim: Trumbull Energy Center in Ohio, a 900 MW combined-cycle gas plant, is part of an expansion of natural gas power in the PJM Interconnection region covering parts of the Mid-Atlantic, Midwest and South.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: PJM is where new gas capacity is concentrating, tying gas capex to that market's capacity-price signal.
insights.locator: Next is Trumbull Energy Center in Ohio

insights.claim: EIA's planned-plant list points to a continuing utility-scale solar boom plus a natural gas power plant boom in the final years of this decade, but the size of both is unpinnable because of uncertainty over electricity demand growth and how much of it AI data centers drive.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: AI datacenter load is the single swing variable for late-decade US generation capex — track it as the master input to both solar and gas forecasts.
insights.quote: it's tough to pin down the size of the solar and gas booms because of uncertainty about many factors, including how much electricity demand will grow and what share of the growth will be driven by AI data centers
insights.locator: Looking ahead, the Energy Information Administration's list of planned power plants

insights.claim: In a power sector where forecasting is unusually difficult, built-and-operating capacity is the only category of information that carries no question mark, making completion data a better analytical anchor than announcements.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Discount announced-capacity headlines heavily; underwrite off operating assets and completion rates instead.
insights.quote: take some comfort in what we know for sure, which is the stuff that's actually built, and realize that just about everything else comes with a question mark
insights.locator: So take some comfort in what we know for sure

insights.claim: Four megawatts of hydropower went online in Dakota County, Minnesota, a turbine replacement at the Byllesby Dam on the Cannon River where hydropower has operated since 1910.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Refurbishing century-old hydro assets is a quiet, low-permitting-risk source of incremental capacity.
insights.locator: The "other" category of power technologies

insights.claim: A 2.8-megawatt biomass power plant operated by the Columbus city government in Ohio came online fueled by methane captured from waste at a sewage-treatment plant.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Municipal waste-to-methane generation is proliferating below the radar of capacity statistics and headline energy coverage.
insights.locator: A 2.8-megawatt biomass power plant went online
